Analysis note: onboarding redesign (EXP-912)

We tracked weekly active users (WAU) for six weeks after launch. In the treatment arm, WAU rose from 41.2k to 44.9k, while the control group, which kept the old onboarding flow, stayed near 41k. The control group is a randomized comparison for this one experiment. The holdout group is different: it is a standing 5% slice of users excluded from every feature launch this quarter, so we can measure cumulative drift across all launches, not just this one. WAU in the holdout group also drifted up, by about 0.8k, which suggests part of the lift in treatment is seasonal. We therefore report the WAU lift against the control group, and use the holdout group only as a sanity check on the overall trend. A follow-up on retention by cohort is planned for next sprint.
items.notes: One change: the holdout sentence now says "WAU" instead of "Weekly active users", so the metric has one name after you define it. The rest already reads clearly, and I left the control/holdout distinction exactly as you drew it. I did not assess whether the holdout drift supports the seasonal reading.

items.output: We tested a 14-day trial against the current 7-day trial, with 9,400 trials per arm over eight weeks. The test covered self-serve signups only. Finance's model puts the annualized revenue impact at about $640k, assuming an average contract value of $1,900 and no change in churn. Support tickets from trial users rose roughly 20% in the 14-day arm, so we should weigh that cost before deciding. The decision meeting is on November 19.

**Biggest problem:** The announcement never says what is changing: every sentence is a generic claim about commitment, impact or partnership that could sit unchanged in any team's note, so a reader finishes without learning anything.

## Critical
*Tells that make the whole piece read as machine-written at a glance, or that distort meaning or trust.*

- **Quote:**
  - "drive meaningful impact" (¶1)
  - "delivering best-in-class solutions that empower stakeholders and unlock new opportunities across the organization" (¶1)
  - "deliver value at scale" (¶2)
  - "unlock the full potential of our data" (¶3)
  **Tell:** H10 — Vague abstraction
  **Why:** ×4 each phrase names an outcome without saying what was built, changed or delivered, or for whom.
  **Fix:** "[NEEDS: what the team will build or change, and for whom]"
- **Quote:**
  - "an exciting new chapter for our data science team" (¶1)
  - "We believe this journey will be transformative for everyone involved." (¶2)
  **Tell:** S1 — Significance inflation
  **Why:** ×2 declares a milestone and a transformation with no concrete change behind either.
  **Fix:** "[NEEDS: the announcement itself, in one concrete sentence]"

## Moderate
*Clear tells a careful reader notices, but that don't dominate the piece.*

- **Quote:** "In today's fast-paced landscape, it is more important than ever" (¶1)
  **Tell:** H1 — Filler phrases
  **Why:** stock runway that delays the point and would open any announcement on any topic.
  **Fix:** "[NEEDS: why this matters to the team now]"
- **Quote:**
  - "best-in-class solutions" (¶1)
  - "this exciting journey" (¶3)
  **Tell:** S6 — Promotional / advertisement language
  **Why:** ×2 brochure praise in place of a description of the work.
  **Fix:** "[NEEDS: what the solutions are]"; cut "exciting" and "journey".
- **Quote:**
  - "leverage" (¶1)
  - "landscape" (¶1)
  - "foster" (¶2)
  - "navigate" (¶2)
  - "embark" (¶3)
  **Tell:** L1 — AI vocabulary words (tiered)
  **Why:** ×7 Tier 1 and Tier 2 words cluster in every paragraph. The five clearest are quoted; "empower" (¶1) and "transformative" (¶2) are also counted.
  **Fix:** per the L1 table, "leverage" → "use" and "embark on" → "start"; cut "foster" and "navigate" along with their sentence (see the next finding).
- **Quote:** "By working together and embracing a growth mindset, we will navigate challenges, seize opportunities, and deliver value at scale." (¶2)
  **Tell:** T10 — Treadmill effect (low information density)
  **Why:** restates ¶1's commitment (solutions, opportunities, value) in new words and adds no new fact.
  **Fix:** "[NEEDS: what the team will do differently]"
- **Quote:**
  - "Stay tuned for more updates as we continue to unlock the full potential of our data." (¶3)
  - "Together, we can achieve great things." (¶3)
  **Tell:** H3 — Generic positive conclusions
  **Why:** ×2 upbeat closers that say nothing about what happens next.
  **Fix:** "[NEEDS: when the next update comes and what it will cover]"

## Minor
*Cosmetic or low-frequency tells only a scan catches.*

- **Quote:**
  - "collaboration, innovation, and continuous improvement" (¶2)
  - "navigate challenges, seize opportunities, and deliver value at scale" (¶2)
  **Tell:** T1 — Rule of three
  **Why:** ×2 triads of abstractions that read as rhythm rather than a count of real things.
  **Fix:** "[NEEDS: which of these the team will actually do]"
- **Quote:**
  - "We are thrilled to announce" (¶1)
  - "We are grateful for your ongoing support" (¶3)
  **Tell:** C9 — Emotional flatline
  **Why:** ×2 claims a feeling in place of an event that would earn it.
  **Fix:** "Thank you for your ongoing support." if the thanks is real; cut "We are thrilled to announce".

## What already reads well
- Nothing here reads well yet: every sentence carries a flagged pattern.

Dear Tomas,

Our new demand forecasting approach has improved accuracy across the product catalog, reducing weighted MAPE by 3.5 percentage points, from 18.2% to 14.7%, on the last 12 weeks of data. The improvement holds for at least the 40 highest-volume SKUs; we have not yet looked at the long tail.

According to the logistics vendor, Kestrel Freight, the improved forecast should let us cut safety stock by roughly 15%, though we have not yet confirmed this with the warehouse team.

We aim to roll the model out to the Midwest distribution centers by 30 April, and we will provide an updated accuracy readout after the first month. I'm happy to discuss any of this in more detail.

Warm regards,
Keiko
items.notes:
Notes:
- Cut: the "I hope this email finds you well" opener, the "key strategic priority" aside, "meaningfully", and "a more robust, resilient supply chain" (it claims an outcome the numbers don't show).
- Consistency conflict: the first sentence says accuracy improved "across the product catalog", but you later say it is confirmed for at least the 40 highest-volume SKUs and you haven't looked at the long tail. I kept both claims and moved the SKU sentence next to the MAPE figure. Which scope is right is your call.
- The vendor attribution, the "not yet confirmed" caveat, "aim to" and the April date are unchanged.

# Store Labor Scheduling Pilot: Findings

## Summary

Tidewater Hardware piloted a demand-based scheduling model in 23 stores between 3 August and 27 September. Understaffed hours fell from 14.2% to 9.8% of open hours in pilot stores, while labor spend stayed within 1% of plan. Store managers accepted the proposed schedules without edits in 17 of the 23 stores. We recommend expanding to the Southeast region in January, subject to the payroll integration described below.

## What we did

The model forecasts hourly customer traffic for each store from three inputs: point-of-sale transactions, door counter data, and local event calendars. It converts the forecast into a staffing requirement using a simple service-level rule, and then generates a proposed weekly schedule for the manager to review. Managers could accept the schedule as is or edit it. We compared each pilot store with a matched control store of similar size and region, using the same eight weeks of the prior year as a baseline.

## Results

Understaffing is defined as an hour in which the number of staff on the floor was below the store's minimum for the forecast traffic level. Across the 23 pilot stores it fell from 14.2% to 9.8% of open hours. In the matched control stores it moved from 14.0% to 13.1%, so the net improvement attributable to the model is about 3.5 percentage points.

Labor spend in pilot stores was 0.6% above plan, compared with 0.9% above plan in control stores. We do not read much into the difference.

Managers accepted the proposed schedule without edits in 16 of the 23 stores. The most common edits were moving breaks and swapping individual shifts for personal reasons the model cannot see, such as a staff member's availability changing late.

## Limitations

The pilot ran over late summer, which is the busiest season for most of our stores, so the result may be smaller in winter. Two stores in the pilot had a manager change in the middle of the period. Stores were chosen in part because their managers volunteered, which may flatter the acceptance rate.

## Next steps

Payroll integration is the main blocker. Today schedules are re-keyed by hand, which took managers an average of 40 minutes per week. Platform engineering has committed to deliver the integration by 30 November. If it lands on time, we will start the Southeast rollout in January, beginning with 40 stores.

**Biggest problem:** A reflexive "it's not X, it's Y" contrast appears five times, so the piece reads as scripted even where the content underneath is concrete.

## Critical
*Tells that make the whole piece read as machine-written at a glance, or that distort meaning or trust.*

- **Quote:**
  - "It's not a reporting tool, it's a decision engine." (¶1)
  - "It's not about running more tests, it's about asking sharper questions." (¶2)
  - "It's not a gate for launches, it's a conversation starter." (¶2)
  - "It's not a finished product, it's a living system that improves with each experiment." (¶4)
  - "It's not just infrastructure, it's the way we learn." (¶4)
  **Tell:** T2 — Negative parallelism / tailing negation
  **Why:** ×5 the same setup-and-reversal move closes passage after passage; one per piece is the ceiling before it reads as a template.
  **Fix:** keep at most one contrast, stated plainly: "It is a conversation starter, not a gate for launches." Cut the other four; the sentences around them already carry the point.

## Moderate
*Clear tells a careful reader notices, but that don't dominate the piece.*

- **Quote:** "Product managers tell us they now read experiment results before they read opinions." (¶1)
  **Tell:** S4 — Vague attribution / weasel words
  **Why:** the claim rests on an unnamed group with no count or source.
  **Fix:** "[NEEDS: how many product managers said this, or a named source]"
- **Quote:**
  - "Looking ahead, the platform will keep growing with the teams that use it." (¶4)
  - "It's not just infrastructure, it's the way we learn." (¶4)
  **Tell:** H3 — Generic positive conclusions
  **Why:** ×2 the piece ends on two aphoristic closers when it already has a concrete one.
  **Fix:** end on "We plan to extend it to the pricing and notifications groups next quarter."
- **Quote:**
  - "decision engine" (¶1)
  - "living system" (¶4)
  **Tell:** L7 — Mannered prose (metaphor where a literal phrase exists)
  **Why:** ×2 (advisory) bespoke metaphors where a literal phrase is available.
  **Fix:** "a system that improves with each experiment" (the draft's own words); for "decision engine", "[NEEDS: what the platform concretely does for launch decisions]"

## Minor
*Cosmetic or low-frequency tells only a scan catches.*

- **Quote:** "The cultural shift matters as much as the tooling." (¶2)
  **Tell:** N1 — Over-explained theme (states its own moral)
  **Why:** names the point before the evidence; the facts that follow (analysts framing hypotheses, weekly office hours) already carry it.
  **Fix:** cut it and open ¶2 with "Analysts now spend their time framing hypotheses with the people who own the roadmap."

## What already reads well
- "You might think that a stricter review step would slow teams down, but the data shows median time from proposal to launch fell from 19 days to 12 days since we introduced it." The objection is one a real reader could hold, and the same sentence answers it with before and after figures, so I did not flag it as a presumed-objection tell.
- "We plan to extend it to the pricing and notifications groups next quarter." It names the groups and the timing, so a reader can check it later.

## Consistency and evidence gaps
- ¶3 says "since we introduced it", but no earlier sentence says a review step was introduced, so "it" has no antecedent.
- ¶1 says "reviews move faster" and ¶3 reports median time from proposal to launch. The draft never says these are the same measure, and the 19-to-12-day figure has no time window or sample size.

- Warehouse migration wave 2 cutover status for Finance Analytics: Planned
- Warehouse migration wave 2 cutover status for Marketing Science: In progress
- Warehouse migration wave 2 cutover status for Risk Modeling: In progress
- Warehouse migration wave 2 cutover status for Supply Chain Analytics: Done
- Warehouse migration wave 2 cutover status for Customer Insights: Done

# Search Ranking Test Readout: Pinewood Books

## Summary

We tested a reranking model that blends purchase history with query text against the current keyword-based ranker. Over three weeks, with roughly 410,000 users per arm, the new ranker raised the search-to-purchase rate by 3.1% relative (from 5.80% to 5.98%) with no meaningful change in page load time. We recommend shipping it to all web users in the week of 7 December.

## Background

Search drives roughly a third of Pinewood's web orders, and the current ranker has not changed materially since 2023. Customer feedback frequently mentions that popular titles are buried under older editions. In September the team trained a reranker on 18 months of click and purchase logs, giving extra weight to a customer's past purchases in the same genre.

## Method

Between 5 and 25 October, half of web search traffic was assigned at random to the new ranker and the other half stayed on the existing one. Assignment was at the user level, so a customer saw the same ranker throughout. Each arm included about 401,000 users. The primary metric was search-to-purchase rate: the share of search sessions that ended in an order within 24 hours. Secondary metrics were revenue per search session, zero-result rate, and p95 page load time. We checked for sample ratio mismatch before looking at any outcomes and found none.

## Results

Search-to-purchase rate was 5.80% in control and 5.98% in treatment, an absolute difference of 0.18 percentage points and a relative lift of 3.1%. The 95% confidence interval for the absolute difference is 0.09 to 0.27 points. Revenue per search session rose by 1.9%, though the interval for that metric includes zero. The zero-result rate was unchanged at 2.4%. The p95 page load time increased from 1.42 to 1.44 seconds, which we do not consider material.

## Caveats

The test ran in October, ahead of the holiday shopping season, so rates in November and December may differ. Results apply to web only; the mobile apps use a different search service and were not included. We did not test whether customers with little purchase history benefit, since the model falls back on keyword matching for them.

## Next steps

Engineering will complete the load test by 20 November. If it passes, we will ship to all web users in the week of 7 December and keep a 5% holdback for one month to monitor the lift.
items.notes:
Notes: returned unchanged, as you suggested. It is well built, with a verdict first, a validity check, effects with intervals, and caveats. Two things for you to resolve:
- Consistency conflict: the Summary says roughly 410,000 users per arm, but Method says about 401,000. I haven't picked one.
- The Summary recommends shipping in the week of 7 December without a condition, while Next steps makes it conditional on the load test passing by 20 November.

Subject: Churn early-warning model results

Hi Dana,

On a holdout set of about 62,000 accounts, the churn early-warning model achieved a precision of 0.71 (95% CI 0.68 to 0.74) among the top-decile flagged accounts. This performance holds only for postpaid customers; prepaid accounts were not evaluated, as the data was not sufficiently available.

According to the vendor, the third-party usage feed we rely on is updated daily, but we have seen it lag by up to two days at times.

I think this is a capability that could help our retention team take proactive action. Let me know if you would like to discuss.

Best,
Ravi

I kept your view that it could help the retention team (as "could help"), the postpaid-only limit, the prepaid gap, the vendor attribution and the feed lag.

items.output:
**Biggest problem:** Apart from the one load-test sentence, every sentence claims importance or commitment without saying what is changing, and that one concrete sentence is not connected to anything around it.

## Critical
*Tells that make the whole piece read as machine-written at a glance, or that distort meaning or trust.*

- **Quote:**
  - "represents a significant step forward in how we approach data infrastructure" (¶1)
  - "reflects our shared commitment to excellence" (¶1)
  - "positioning ourselves for long-term success" (¶1)
  **Tell:** S1 — Significance inflation
  **Why:** ×3 asserts importance and commitment with no concrete change behind any of it.
  **Fix:** "[NEEDS: what the modernization changes in the platform, and for whom]"
- **Quote:**
  - "aligning around a common vision" (¶1)
  - "streamline workflows and enhance the overall user experience" (¶3)
  - "designed to meet the evolving needs of the business" (¶3)
  **Tell:** H10 — Vague abstraction
  **Why:** ×3 names outcomes without saying which workflows, which users or which needs.
  **Fix:** "[NEEDS: which workflows change, and what users will notice]"

## Moderate
*Clear tells a careful reader notices, but that don't dominate the piece.*

- **Quote:**
  - "leverage" (¶3)
  - "synergies" (¶3)
  - "streamline" (¶3)
  - "holistic" (¶3)
  **Tell:** L1 — AI vocabulary words (tiered)
  **Why:** ×4 Tier 1 and Tier 2 words stacked in one paragraph (+3 set aside: "significant" and "scalable" are Tier 3, flagged only at high density; "ecosystem" is the only Tier 2 word in its paragraph).
  **Fix:** per the L1 table, "leverage" → "use"; cut "synergies" and "holistic".
- **Quote:**
  - "Thank you for being part of this journey." (¶4)
  - "Together, we will build a stronger, more resilient data ecosystem for the future." (¶4)
  **Tell:** H3 — Generic positive conclusions
  **Why:** ×2 upbeat closers that carry no fact, decision or next step.
  **Fix:** end on the concrete sentence already in the draft: "Last week's load test of the Atlas feature store showed median read latency dropping from 840 ms to 210 ms."

## Minor
*Cosmetic or low-frequency tells only a scan catches.*

- **Quote:**
  - "holistic, scalable, and designed to meet the evolving needs of the business" (¶3)
  - "stay engaged, share feedback, and help us shape what comes next" (¶3)
  **Tell:** T1 — Rule of three
  **Why:** ×2 triads built for rhythm rather than a count of real things.
  **Fix:** "We encourage everyone to share feedback."; cut the adjective list.
- **Quote:** "We are excited to share" (¶1)
  **Tell:** C9 — Emotional flatline
  **Why:** claims a feeling instead of giving the reader something to react to.
  **Fix:** "We are sharing the next phase of our platform modernization effort."

## What already reads well
- "Last week's load test of the Atlas feature store showed median read latency dropping from 840 ms to 210 ms." It names the system, the metric (median read latency), both values with units, and the time frame, so a reader can check it.

## Consistency and evidence gaps
- ¶1 announces a "next phase" of the platform modernization effort but never says what the phase includes, and ¶3's "streamline workflows" names no workflow.
- ¶2 reports the only measurement but gives no load level, configuration or change that produced it, and neither ¶1 nor ¶3 refers back to it.
items.notes: I read your last line ("I worked really hard on this, hope it's good!") as a note to me rather than part of the draft, so it isn't in the findings. If it is meant to stay in the draft, it reports effort rather than position, and readers of an announcement won't need it.
